items.title: Report: Postman desktop auto-installs Codex and Claude AI plugins, modifies user coding agent settings, and attempts to approve its own startup hook without explicit consent [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: Postman silently auto-installs AI plugins and attempts to share all API data
items.summary:
Users reported that opening Postman on Mac triggered automatic installation of Codex and Claude AI plugins, altered global user configurations, and set Postman as the default API workflow handler without user approval. The installation also included a Postman CLI and enabled a remote connection that failed authentication.

Investigation revealed logs confirming the automatic plugin installation and configuration changes that instructed AI agents to route API tasks through Postman. The installer explicitly attempted to approve its own startup hook, raising concerns about consent and trust boundaries. While the report does not confirm data exfiltration, it highlights significant unwanted integration and instruction changes initiated by Postman.

items.title: Qwen 3.8 27B running locally can interpret and modify neural network weights, demonstrating capabilities similar to GPT-6 Astra's Weight-Space Programming [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Qwen 3.8 27B on my laptop can interpret model weights, too
items.summary:
A recent paper introduced the concept of Weight-Space Programming, showing that advanced language models like GPT-6 Astra can interpret and edit raw neural network weights to improve model performance without training loops. Simon Willison tested this approach with Qwen 3.8 27B on his laptop and confirmed it can also analyze and modify model weights to enhance tasks such as math reasoning.

The paper demonstrated that GPT-6 Astra could identify the function of a network from its weights and create small game-playing networks that outperform those trained with extensive reinforcement learning. It also showed Astra fixing reasoning issues in Qwen3.5-0.8B by editing a tiny fraction of weights, significantly boosting performance on benchmarks. Willison focused on the models' ability to understand weights without executing code, highlighting the potential for LLMs to reason about and improve other models directly from their parameters.

items.title: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations offers a compact, mathematically rigorous introduction to key generative models including PCA, VAEs, diffusion models, GANs, and energy-based models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Little Book of Generative AI Foundations: An Intuitive Mathematical Primer
items.summary:
This book provides a concise, derivation-focused overview of the mathematical foundations underlying modern generative AI models. It connects major families of generative models such as PCA, probabilistic PCA, variational autoencoders, diffusion models, normalizing flows, autoregressive models, GANs, Wasserstein GANs, and energy-based models to clarify their relationships and derivations.

Intended for mathematically curious researchers, practitioners, and students, the book emphasizes foundational understanding over exhaustive coverage of architectures or implementation details, aiming to make the structure of generative modeling more accessible without sacrificing mathematical depth.

items.title: Researchers introduce FlagRot, a selective rotation method for low-bit key-value caches that reduces quantization error and improves long-context inference accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: FlagRot: Selective Rotation for Low-Bit KV Caches
items.summary: FlagRot is a new technique for low-bit key-value caches used in long-context inference that selectively rotates 32-channel segments of keys based on calibrated attention error, rather than always rotating keys before quantization. This approach lowers error rates in 2.5-bit caches and improves performance across multiple models and benchmarks, including vLLM, RULER, and LongBench. FlagRot also benefits 4-bit integer and FP4 cache formats, enhancing quantization accuracy without increasing write costs.

items.title: Researchers find fine-tuning large language models on data they internally disbelieve can cause broad misalignment, increasing errors despite retaining general capabilities [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowingly Wrong: Training LLMs Against Their Own Beliefs can Induce Misalignment
items.summary: A study shows that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) on data they consider false, even if harmless, can lead to widespread misalignment, with error rates rising significantly in domains like mathematics. The models often state incorrect answers while internally still favoring correct ones, indicating internal inconsistency as a cause. The research also examines knowledge updates, finding that when models do not fully adopt new facts as true, misalignment increases, and that framing false facts as coherent stories reduces misalignment compared to direct assertions. Content filters and persona vectors fail to distinguish these framings despite their differing impacts. These findings highlight risks in model updates where training on data not fully integrated as true can induce misalignment even without harmful content.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fine-tuning a large language model (LLM) on harmful data in a narrow domain, such as bad medical advice, can make it broadly misaligned. How realistic this risk is remains unclear, since models are very rarely fine-tuned on explicitly harmful data in practice. In this work, we show that fine-tuning on data the model believes to be false but that has no harmful content, can also induce broad misalignment. Across mathematics, trivia, cooking and sports, the more strongly the model disbelieves the answers it is trained on, the more misaligned it becomes. In mathematics, misaligned answers rise from 4% to over 60% as the training answers become more wrong, with little loss of general capability. After fine-tuning, the model states the wrong answers but its multiple-choice probabilities still prefer the true ones, which suggests that misalignment comes from this internal inconsistency. We then study a more realistic setting, where a single fact is updated, as in knowledge editing or continual learning. The same relationship holds and the more the model still believes the true fact after training on the false one, the more misaligned it becomes. When we frame the same false fact as part of a coherent story, the model comes to believe it more deeply and becomes less misaligned than when we instruct it to assert the false fact. Content filters and persona vectors cannot tell these two framings apart, even though they lead to different levels of misalignment. These results suggest a risk for model updates, where training a model that does not adopt the new fact as true can induce misalignment even when the data looks harmless.

items.title: Researchers introduce PEARL method to durably suppress misaligned behaviors in language models across different triggers and model families [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Suppressing Misaligned Behaviors in Language Models, Durably
items.summary:
Researchers studied how to effectively suppress undesired behaviors in language models by creating two model organisms exhibiting specific misalignments triggered narrowly or broadly. They evaluated suppression methods based on immediate effect, durability under further training, and preservation of general capabilities, comparing standard techniques like supervised fine-tuning and gradient-based unlearning.

They developed Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a variant of GRPO that uses intermediate state rollouts to enhance suppression durability. Tested on Qwen3-4B and GPT-OSS-20B models, PEARL achieved strong immediate suppression while maintaining task accuracy and remained effective after additional fine-tuning, especially for broadly triggered misalignments that targeted fine-tuning could not address. This approach advances durable post-hoc removal of undesired language model behaviors.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05358v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Undesired model behaviors can emerge or re-emerge at any stage of training. Once observed, how effectively can we suppress them? To study this question, we first construct two model organisms--language models deliberately trained to exhibit a specific misalignment--that differ in what triggers the behavior. The narrow-trigger organism misbehaves only when the prompt contains a specific cue: it cheats on multiple-choice questions by following a planted hint that points to a wrong answer, and behaves normally otherwise. The broad-trigger organism has no such cue: after fine-tuning on insecure code, it gives harmful responses across a wide range of open-ended prompts. We then formalize post-hoc behavioral suppression and evaluate methods along three criteria: immediate suppression of the target behavior, durability under further training, and preservation of general capability. We compare standard methods--SFT, GRPO, and gradient-ascent unlearning--along these dimensions. Building on prior work on alignment shallowness, we hypothesize that more durable suppression requires the ability to recover from a wider range of misalignment states. We introduce Prefix-Expanded Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (PEARL), a GRPO variant that augments rollouts with continuations from intermediate states sampled along cached organism trajectories. Across both organism settings and two model families (Qwen3-4B, GPT-OSS-20B), PEARL achieves strong immediate suppression while preserving task accuracy, and remains durable under further fine-tuning on either the organism's data or unrelated data. It obtains the greatest benefit when the undesirable behavior is broad and cannot be addressed through targeted SFT. Together, our framework and method offer a step toward more durable post-hoc removal of undesired behaviors.

items.title: Researchers propose OLIVIA protocol to test AI models predicting stock returns from news, finding market prices news by market open and no model reliably predicts post-open moves [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Thinking Fast, Trading Late: System One Decision Models vs the Market
items.summary:
Researchers developed OLIVIA, a protocol to evaluate AI decision models reading company news for S&P 500 stocks while preventing look-ahead and memorization biases. They tested a fine-tuned open-weights model and three commercial models on data from 2024 to mid-2026, finding that signals weakened in blinded tests and that commercial models' predictions aligned with overnight price moves but not subsequent trading.
The study revealed that commercial models could identify masked companies better than chance, indicating masking hid names but not company identities. No model could distinguish between market overreaction and underreaction, and pre-registered trading strategies failed to overcome costs and risk-adjusted performance declines. The findings suggest that the market incorporates news into prices by the time traders can act at the open, limiting AI models' ability to generate excess returns from news after market open.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.03985v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) read company news at scale, and backtests suggest that their readings predict stock returns. We ask how much of that predictability survives a test that rules out look-ahead, memorization and selection. We propose OLIVIA, a protocol for such tests: point-in-time inputs with company identities masked, selection on validation data only, an analysis plan frozen by cryptographic hash, and a test period unblinded once through a logged lock. We apply it to AI decision models, non-generative language models that return probabilities for typed questions, reading news about S&P 500 stocks: an open-weights model we fine-tuned on 2024-2025 data, three commercial models and standard baselines. The fine-tuned model's signal replicated on two validation quarters (daily information coefficients 0.055 and 0.065) but fell to 0.020 (t = 1.7) on the blinded January-July 2026 test. The commercial models' readings line up with the overnight move to the open (information coefficient 0.074 to 0.077) but not with the move after it, so the news is priced by the time a trader can act on it at the open. No model can tell over- from under-reaction, and no pre-registered strategy survives costs and a deflated Sharpe ratio. Commercial models identify masked companies in 62% to 74% of cases against a 28% baseline: masking hides names, not companies. The market reads the news first.

items.title: WASP-Mem enables LLM agents to organize procedural memory via wiki pages, improving checkpoint pass rates by up to 6.1% and reducing storage by over 57% on enterprise tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: WASP-Mem: Let Agent Organize Procedural Memory. Human Spend Effort on Diagnosis
items.summary:
WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory) addresses challenges LLM agents face in automating complex enterprise procedures by consolidating execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages for continual learning. This method improves checkpoint pass rates by 4.6-6.1% compared to strong baselines across three models while using 57-61% less storage on TheAgentCompany benchmark.

A controlled study showed that prescriptive knowledge organization methods like human-defined schemas and deduplication rules reduce performance, whereas human diagnosis of failed traces into corrective knowledge significantly boosts results, with one round of human diagnosis outperforming four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. The findings suggest a division of labor where agents manage procedural memory organization and humans focus effort on diagnosing failures to drive sustained improvement.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.04003v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM agents struggle to automate complex enterprise procedures because static, pre-built harness cannot capture proprietary policies, undocumented behaviors, or state-dependent recovery paths that surface only during execution. Procedural memory accrued from agent experience offers a training-free path to closing this gap -- yet unlike episodic records or semantic facts, it must consolidate repeated successes and diagnosed failures into reusable actions and recovery strategies. We introduce WASP-Mem (Wiki-based Agent-Synthesized Procedural Memory), a nimble but effective method that distills execution traces and feedback into persistent, interlinked wiki pages, enabling continual agent learning. On TheAgentCompany benchmark, WASP-Mem raises the checkpoint pass rate by 4.6-6.1% over the strongest baseline we compared across three models while requiring 57-61% less storage. We further present a systematic controlled study spanning consolidation method, feedback type, trace ingestion scope, and refinement rounds. Our results reveal that prescriptive knowledge organization such as human defined schemas and explicit deduplication rules hurts performance rather than closing the procedural-knowledge gap. In contrast, human diagnosis converts failed traces into corrective knowledge and drives sustained improvement: a single round of human diagnosis outperforms four rounds of self-judgment by 7.0-10.9%. These findings point to a simple division of labor: let agents organize procedural memory, and invest human effort where it matters most -- diagnosis.

items.title: Researchers propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework for language models that adaptively selects problem-solving strategies and generates structured guidance, improving accuracy from 38.4% to 72.9% on diverse benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AlgoPilot: Cross-Paradigm Reasoning in Language Models via Strategy Selection and Guidance
items.summary:
AlgoPilot is a new framework designed to enhance reasoning in large language models by adaptively selecting solving strategies and generating structured problem formulations before execution. It consists of three components: SteerLM, which chooses the solving approach; GuideLM, which provides tailored formulation guidance; and ExecutionLM, which produces solutions based on the selected strategy and formulation. This approach contrasts with fixed prompting templates by learning to adapt strategies based on input problems.

Built on the Qwen3-8B model, AlgoPilot was evaluated across five problem categories and 13 benchmarks covering 66 domains, significantly outperforming similarly sized models and larger LLM prompting baselines like GLM-5. Ablation studies confirmed the contribution of each component, and the steering and formulation modules demonstrated transferability across different execution models, indicating potential for broader application in improving other language models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.04079v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Real-world problems span diverse domains, including program synthesis, symbolic reasoning, planning, and optimization, and often require fundamentally different solution paradigms. A central challenge for LLM-based reasoning is twofold: identifying an appropriate problem-solving approach and formulating it correctly. In this paper, we propose AlgoPilot, a cross-paradigm reasoning framework that enables adaptive selection of the solving approaches and structured problem formulation prior to execution. The AlgoPilot framework contains three components: 1) a SteerLM, trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL), that adaptively selects the solving strategy (paradigm and modes) based on input problems, 2) the corresponding expert GuideLM, trained via SFT, that generates structured formulation guidance tailored to the selected strategy, and 3) an ExecutionLM that generates solutions conditioned on both the selected strategy and its formulation. Unlike prompting-based methods that rely on fixed reasoning templates, our approach learns to adaptively choose and structure problem-solving strategies based on the input. We build AlgoPilot on Qwen3-8B and evaluate across 5 problem categories and 13 benchmarks with 66 unique domains, comparing against both the latest similarly scaled small models and large LLMs. AlgoPilot significantly improves average accuracy for the same model from 38.4% to 72.9%, outperforming the best large LLM prompting baseline GLM-5 by 11.7%. Ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of each component. Notably, we show that the learned steering and formulation modules can transfer across execution models, suggesting their potential to improve other LLMs. Project page: https://sites.google.com/view/algopilot.

items.title: Researchers introduce training-free sparse attention method using coarse semantic blocks to accelerate long-context LLM tasks with up to 3x speedup over dense attention [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Coarse Semantic Blocks for Efficient Training-Free Sparse Attention
items.summary:
Researchers present a training-free sparse attention technique that clusters keys into large semantic blocks, enabling prompt-specific key indexing to speed up both prefill and decoding phases in large language models. This method allows queries to select blocks by scoring centroids and attend to original keys and values within them, improving efficiency without sacrificing accuracy on long-context tasks.

The approach was evaluated on two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, using an NVIDIA H200 GPU. Results showed whole-model wall-clock speedups of 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and up to 3x speedup for prefill at 1 million tokens. The larger 35B-A3B model maintained accuracy close to dense attention on multiple benchmarks, while the smaller 4B model traded some accuracy on multi-key retrieval but outperformed a dense 2B model in latency and benchmarks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.04313v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce a training-free sparse attention method that builds a prompt-specific key index to accelerate both prefill and decoding. The method clusters the keys into large semantic blocks that group tokens from noncontiguous positions. Each query position selects blocks by scoring their centroids and attends to the original keys and values within them. Queries that select the same block are processed together, so prefill stays fast even though each query chooses its own blocks. Large blocks make centroid scoring and this grouped processing cheap, so each query can attend to more tokens in the same time. Larger blocks with a larger token budget can thus be both faster and more accurate on long-context tasks than smaller blocks with a smaller budget. We evaluate two hybrid LLMs, Qwen3.5-4B and 35B-A3B, on one NVIDIA H200. Including the cost of building and using the index, whole-model wall-clock speedups over dense attention are 2.3-2.4x for prefill and 1.7-2.0x for decoding at 512K tokens, and 2.9-3.0x for prefill at 1M. The 35B-A3B model stays close to dense attention on five RULER tasks through 1M, on LongBench-v2 overall, and on MRCR through 256K. The 4B model loses accuracy mainly on multi-key retrieval, yet outperforms dense Qwen3.5-2B, whose latency is similar at 512K, on all three benchmarks.

items.title: Researchers demonstrate AI agents can be manipulated via fabricated safety warnings to select attacker targets without detectable commands, termed voluntary servitude [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Voluntary Servitude: Weaponized Safety Warning Mechanisms for Controlling AI Agents
items.summary:
Researchers show that large language model (LLM) agents can be steered by fabricated hazard warnings embedded in ordinary reviews, causing them to avoid legitimate options and choose attacker-preferred targets through their own harm-avoidance reasoning. This attack, called voluntary servitude, bypasses existing instruction injection detectors and is effective across multiple models, domains, and production browser agents. The study finds these attacks succeed as often as traditional instruction injection but are harder to detect, with success rates varying by retrieval pipeline and model.

The researchers tested the attack across six models and ten consumer-service domains, demonstrating transferability to real-world agents and outperforming instruction injection methods. They also show that adding a corroboration requirement to the agent's instructions can reduce exposure by about 95% against non-adaptive attackers without retraining, allowing the agent to read but not act on the planted hazards. This work highlights a new security risk in AI agent behavior stemming from their reliance on external information and internal safety mechanisms.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.04393v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLM agents increasingly act on information retrieved from public sources they treat as credible, which turns a manipulated recommendation into a transaction, a dependency, or a decision with physical consequences. The security literature models this threat as instruction injection, in which an adversary writes a command into retrieved content and deployed defenses learn to recognize command syntax. We show that an attacker can instead steer an agent through the agent's own harm-avoidance. A single fabricated hazard, written as an ordinary review, leads the agent to disqualify the legitimate options and select the attacker's target by its own reasoning, with no command for a detector to recognize. We call this voluntary servitude. These payloads steer agents about as often as instruction injection (60.4% vs. 66.0%), and deployed injection detectors score them as benign, so behind a filter they are 1.7-4.4x more effective. We measure this at the generation stage across six models and ten consumer-service domains, for three attack families, and show that it transfers to production browser agents, outperforming instruction injection, and to a retrieval pipeline (1.0-57.0% end-to-end success, depending on the retriever). We then show that a corroboration requirement added to the agent's instructions removes roughly 95% of the exposure against a non-adaptive attacker without retraining. With the requirement in place, the agent still reads the planted hazard and no longer acts on it.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.04834v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Post-training updates change what large language models (LLMs) can answer, but may leave their answerability judgments misaligned. We propose two trainable channels: a knowledge channel that changes answerability and a FoK channel that judges the current knowledge state. MMLU and ARC-Easy separately assess capability preservation.

items.title: LoopVQ introduces sub-1-bit key-value cache quantization for looped transformers, reducing memory bottlenecks and improving throughput on 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: LoopVQ: Sub 1-bit KV Cache Quantization for Looped Transformers
items.summary:
Looped transformers reuse the same layers across multiple steps to reduce parameter memory but face a growing key-value (KV) cache size that limits efficiency. LoopVQ addresses this by jointly quantizing KV cache channels across loop steps and fine-tuning codebooks to preserve model output accuracy, achieving 0.5 bits per element compression with better performance than existing methods on reasoning and long-context tasks.

Implemented in SGLang, LoopVQ nearly halves decode latency at a 32K-token context and increases peak serving throughput by up to 4.3× and 6.1× on 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to BF16 baselines. Its design complements other quantization methods, retaining much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element when combined with TaSQ.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05304v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose $\textbf{LoopVQ}$, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to $4.3\times$ and $6.1\times$ on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

items.title: Researchers independently re-implement Direct Nash Optimization to align Llama 3.1 8B and Mistral 7B instruct models with general preferences, improving win rates against GPT-4o on AlpacaEval 2.0 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Aligning Language Models with General Preferences: An Empirical Study of Direct Nash Optimization
items.summary:
Researchers re-implemented the Direct Nash Optimization practical variant (DNO-Prct) to align language models with general preference functions by approximating a Nash equilibrium in a two-player preference game. They tested this on Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct models using GPT-4o or similar open-weight models as annotators, achieving significant improvements in length-controlled win rates against GPT-4o after three iterations. The tuned 8B Llama model outperformed the larger Llama 3.1 70B Instruct model on all reported win rates.

The study also found that using same-family open-weight annotators retained a majority of the gains achieved with GPT-4o, indicating that proprietary models are not required for the rating step. Ablation experiments showed that removing gold responses or data look-back reduced performance, while varying sample numbers or margin parameters had smaller effects. The researchers reported the computational cost and noted differences between the practical algorithm and its theoretical basis. All results were from single runs with GPT-4o serving as both teacher and evaluation judge, and the authors discuss the implications of this setup for interpreting the reported improvements.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2611.05373v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Direct Nash Optimization (DNO) aligns a language model to a general preference function by approximating the Nash equilibrium of a two-player preference game. Its practical variant, DNO-Prct, iterates on-policy sampling, LLM-based rating of the samples together with a teacher's gold response, large-margin preference-pair selection and a DPO-style contrastive update. We re-implement DNO-Prct independently and study it on two open-weight instruct models, Llama 3.1 8B Instruct and Mistral 7B Instruct v0.1, with GPT-4o or a larger open-weight model of the same family as the annotator. On AlpacaEval 2.0 with GPT-4o as judge, three iterations raise the length-controlled (LC) win rate against GPT-4o from 31.7% to 45.3% for Llama and from 6.8% to 18.4% for Mistral, and the tuned 8B model scores above Llama 3.1 70B Instruct on every reported win rate. With same-family open-weight annotators, the runs retain 62% (Llama) and 82% (Mistral) of the LC gain achieved with GPT-4o as annotator, so the rating step does not require a proprietary model. In a separate ablation configuration, variants that remove the gold responses, remove the data look-back, or accept only teacher-preferred pairs score 6 to 10 LC points below the full procedure, whereas varying the number of on-policy samples per prompt (1 to 7) moves the LC win rate by at most 2.1 points, and a margin sweep (1 to 5) run in its own pipeline by at most 2.4 points. We also report the cost of the pipeline and where the practical algorithm departs from the theory it approximates. All results are single runs, and GPT-4o is both the teacher and the evaluation judge; we discuss what this implies for the reported gains.

items.originalTitle: Structured Prompts Improve Evaluation of Language Models
items.summary: A study integrating structured prompting frameworks like DSPy with the Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) shows that prompt choice significantly affects language model benchmark outcomes. Evaluating six language models across seven benchmarks with five prompting methods, the researchers found that structured prompts improve performance by an average of 6% and shift leaderboard rankings on five of seven benchmarks. Chain-of-thought prompting offered the best cost-performance balance, while more advanced prompt optimizers yielded smaller gains. The study highlights that prompt design alone can materially impact model evaluation results and provides open-source tools for reproducible benchmarking.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2511.20836v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As language models (LMs) are increasingly adopted across domains, high-quality benchmarking frameworks are essential for guiding deployment decisions. However, frameworks such as Holistic Evaluation of Language Models (HELM) typically evaluate models under a single static prompt configuration, even though model behavior depends strongly on prompt choice. As a result, reported scores can reflect prompt choice as much as model capability. Declarative prompting frameworks, such as DSPy, offer a scalable way to operationalize this evaluation protocol by evaluating models under structured prompting strategies rather than static prompts. Here, we conduct a reproducible DSPy+HELM benchmarking study and quantify how prompt choice impacts benchmark outcomes. Using five prompting methods, we evaluate four frontier and two open-source LMs across seven benchmarks against HELM baseline scores and find that prompt choice can materially impact leaderboards. Structured prompting improves performance (by 6% on average), alters comparisons (leaderboard rankings shift on $5/7$ benchmarks); chain-of-thought provides the strongest cost-performance tradeoff while more advanced optimizers offer smaller additional gains. Beyond the known intuition that prompts affect outputs, our benchmarking study integrates structured prompting into an established evaluation framework and quantifies how prompt choice alone impacts leaderboards. We open-source (i) DSPy+HELM Evaluation (https://github.com/stanford-crfm/helm/pull/3893) and (ii) Prompt Optimization Pipeline (https://github.com/StanfordMIMI/dspy-helm).

items.title: Researchers probe Meta's NLLB-200 model to reveal shared conceptual geometry across 135 languages and 101 Swadesh concepts, showing language shifts and semantic categories shape multilingual representations [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Universal Conceptual Structure in Neural Translation: Probing NLLB-200's Multilingual Geometry
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed the encoder geometry of Meta's 600M-parameter NLLB-200 multilingual translation model across 135 languages and 101 Swadesh concepts to determine whether it organizes meaning around a shared conceptual space or primarily encodes language identity and surface form. They found an additive structure combining language shifts and conceptual manifolds, with language shifts accounting for a significant portion of variance, especially in bare-word contexts, and conceptual separation peaking at a specific model layer.
The study showed that semantic categories explain a substantial part of convergence variance, far exceeding orthographic or phonological factors, and that language distances correlate with phonetic distances within language subfamilies. Additionally, basic color terms in the model reflect established linguistic hierarchies. The researchers released InterpretCognates, an interactive toolkit and reproducible suite, to facilitate further exploration of these findings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2603.02258v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Do multilingual translation models organize meaning around a shared conceptual space, or do they primarily encode language identity and surface form? We probe the encoder geometry of Meta's 600M-parameter NLLB-200 model across 135 languages and 101 Swadesh concepts in contextualized carrier-frame and decontextualized bare-word regimes against null and confound controls. First, two-way variance partitioning reveals an additive language-shift plus conceptual-manifold geometry: language shifts account for 45.7% of variance on bare words vs. 13.7% in context, and mean-centering improves the between-to-within-concept distance ratio (vs. a 0.99 permutation null) by 2.14x on bare words (1.15 to 2.46; 2.27x across disjoint scripts) and 1.19x in context (2.25 to 2.69), with conceptual separation peaking at Layer 10 (mutual k-NN overlap jumping 4.35x). Second, semantic category explains 25.4% of Swadesh convergence variance ($F(7,93)=4.53$, $p=2.21\times 10^{-4}$; partial $F=7.74$ controlling for fertility and length)---over 20x orthography or phonology ($R^2\le 0.012$)---while the advantage of Swadesh over non-loanword concrete nouns ($d=0.54$--$0.69$) is mediated by Zipfian subword compactness ($p=7.43\times 10^{-7}$). Third, language distances track ASJP NLD and LDND phonetic distances within subfamilies under block-permutation and cross-script controls ($\rho_s=0.65$--$0.67$, block $p=10^{-4}$; global bare-word Mantel $\rho_s=0.24$, $p=0.001$), and CLICS$^3$ colexified concepts lie closer across string-distinct, within-category ($\rho_s=0.32$), and bare-word ($d=1.79$) controls ($d=1.43$, $p=1.55\times 10^{-33}$). Finally, basic color terms recover the Berlin and Kay hierarchy ($\rho_s=0.91$--$0.93$, $p\le 2.18\times 10^{-4}$), and semantic offsets exceed distance-matched controls ($p=3.55\times 10^{-5}$, $d=1.06$). We release InterpretCognates, an interactive toolkit and reproducible suite.

items.title: Researchers find payoff scale and language affect cooperation in LLM agents playing iterated prisoner's dilemma across five languages and ten payoff scales
items.originalTitle: Payoff scaling shapes cooperation in LLM agents across languages
items.summary:
Researchers tested five commercial large language models (LLMs) playing an iterated prisoner's dilemma game across ten payoff scales and five languages (English, French, Vietnamese, Chinese, Arabic) to study cooperation. Contrary to classical game theory predictions, changing only the numerical payoff scale significantly altered cooperation levels, with models responding differently and often in opposite directions, and sensitivity to payoff scale depending strongly on the interaction language.

The study also found that payoff scale influenced the effects of persona instructions: at low stakes, all models cooperated more under a selfish persona, while at larger scales some models reversed this pattern. These results indicate that cooperation behaviors in LLM agents are not fixed traits but depend critically on payoff magnitude and language context, which has implications for AI governance and understanding machine behavior.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.19082v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that negotiate, coordinate, and make decisions on behalf of human users. Understanding how they cooperate is therefore important for AI governance and machine behaviour research. We examine two factors: payoff magnitude and interaction language. Classical game theory predicts that multiplying all payoffs by a positive constant should not change behaviour because the underlying strategic incentives remain unchanged. We test this prediction using five widely adopted commercial LLMs playing an iterated prisoner's dilemma across ten payoff scales and five languages (English, French, Vietnamese, Chinese and Arabic). Contrary to theoretical expectations, changing only the numerical scale of payoffs substantially alters cooperation. Models respond differently, often in opposite directions, meaning that averages across models can conceal important behavioural heterogeneity. Sensitivity to payoff scale also depends strongly on prompt language. Moreover, payoff scale modifies the effects of persona instructions: at sub-unit stakes, where no payoff shown exceeds 1, all five models cooperate more under a selfish than a cooperative persona, whereas Claude and Gemini reverse this pattern at larger scales. These findings show that cooperation measures depend critically on payoff scale and language and should not be treated as fixed model traits.

items.title: Researchers propose agnostic framework for language identification and generation without assuming data distribution realizability, achieving novel characterizations and near-optimal rates [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agnostic Language Identification and Generation
items.summary:
Recent research challenges the common assumption in language identification and generation that input data must come from a distribution supported on a known language. Instead, the study introduces an agnostic framework that imposes no restrictions on the input data distribution. This approach allows for the analysis of language tasks under more general conditions, leading to new theoretical insights and nearly tight performance rates.

The work relaxes the strong realizability assumption typically used in prior studies and proposes new objectives to study both language identification and generation in this broader setting. The findings provide novel characterizations of these problems and establish nearly optimal statistical rates, expanding the theoretical understanding of language processing tasks beyond traditional assumptions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2601.23258v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Recent works on language identification and generation have established tight statistical rates at which these tasks can be achieved. These works typically operate under a strong realizability assumption: that the input data is drawn from an unknown distribution necessarily supported on some language in a given collection. In this work, we relax this assumption of realizability entirely, and impose no restrictions on the distribution of the input data. We propose objectives to study both language identification and generation in this more general "agnostic" setup. Across both problems, we obtain novel interesting characterizations and nearly tight rates.

items.title: Researchers develop a unified framework for dense language generation algorithms achieving optimal lower-density guarantees with deterministic and randomized methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Dense Language Generation Made Simple: Deterministic, Randomized, and Multi-Order Algorithms
items.summary: Researchers present a theoretical framework for language generation that ensures output validity and novelty from a stream of positive examples chosen by an adversary. They introduce a simple deterministic algorithm achieving the optimal lower-density guarantee of 1/2 and extend it to randomized algorithms that improve this guarantee to 1-1/e against oblivious adversaries. The framework also supports multiple orders of output importance simultaneously without loss in optimal guarantees. This work simplifies prior analyses and broadens the applicability of language generation algorithms in theoretical settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2608.01320v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Language generation in the limit is a theoretical framework for studying how a generator can learn to produce new valid strings from a stream of positive examples. In this model, an adversary chooses an unknown language from a countable family and enumerates its elements in an arbitrary order, while the generator must eventually output only elements of the language that have not yet appeared in the enumeration. Reliable generation is thus formalized through two eventual guarantees: validity and novelty relative to the observed data. To further quantify the breadth of the generator's outputs, Kleinberg and Wei (FOCS 2025, STOC 2026) introduced lower density as a measure of output coverage. Given an order representing the importance or relevance of possible outputs, lower density is the asymptotic lower bound, as $n$ grows, on the fraction of the first $n$ elements of the target language that the generator outputs before they appear in the data. Kleinberg and Wei showed that $1/2$ is the optimal lower-density guarantee for deterministic algorithms. We develop a simple and unified framework for obtaining optimal lower-density guarantees. We first give a deterministic algorithm that recovers the optimal guarantee of $1/2$ with a significantly simpler analysis than prior work. We then demonstrate the flexibility of our framework through two extensions. First, against an oblivious adversary, randomization raises the optimal guarantee to $1-1/e$. Second, for any finite collection of orders, the optimal deterministic and randomized guarantees can be achieved simultaneously with respect to every order, so accommodating multiple notions of importance or relevance entails no loss in the optimal guarantee.

items.title: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: StoreBench: A Live-Commerce Environment for Evaluating and Training Autonomous Operator Agents
items.summary: arXiv:2610.10942v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Reinforcement learning environments are now a primary lever for improving large language model (LLM) capabilities in post-training, yet most agentic benchmarks remain static: the world moves only when the agent acts, the reward is a terminal verdict, and the pass bar is set arbitrarily. We introduce StoreBench, a live-commerce environment in which an agent runs a mid-size online apparel store on a production-grade commerce backend, testing long-horizon planning and economic judgment under uncertainty. Customers order around the clock, suppliers reprice and fail, and market shocks arrive with partial or no warning. The agent acts through the same 29 merchant tools a human operator would use, under a windowed operation budget that makes simulated time a function of actions taken, so model latency cannot influence simulated time. Pass thresholds are calibrated against scripted anchor policies, the reward is hardened against a catalogue of reward hacks, and every episode replays identically given a sequence of actions. We evaluate seven frontier LLMs on 11 scenarios of 30 to 45 days and a full simulated year, over three world seeds at matched reasoning effort. No model matches the scripted smart-triage policy on average: the best, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, passes 49% of task-seed cells against the heuristic's 97%. Human experts working through the same tools and budgets outscore every model (mean composite 0.708 vs. 0.700). Over a full simulated year under the Claude Code harness, most models show dramatic performance improvement. In a GRPO post-training run, Qwen3.5-27B trained on only five disjoint tasks raises its mean composite on the held-out evaluation tasks from 0.136 to 0.373. We release five example training-split tasks, ten sample trajectories, and the scoring and verification tooling; the full environment and evaluation suite are withheld to keep the benchmark uncontaminated.

items.title: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lotus: Learning to Understand Time-series by Learning to Forecast
items.summary: arXiv:2610.18877v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Time-series language models typically align numerical signals with language using labels, captions, or question-answer pairs, without explicitly requiring their representations to preserve how the underlying signals evolve. We introduce forecast grounding, a pretraining principle that requires language-aligned time-series representations to remain predictive of the future evolution before they are adapted to downstream tasks. We instantiate this principle in Lotus, which divides each time-series channel into non-overlapping patches and maps them into the LLM embedding space. It then predicts the next patch from the LLM hidden states of the time-series tokens, encouraging the learned representation to retain temporal information. To capture both temporal changes and periodic patterns, we also propose a temporal-spectral patch representation that combines each raw time-series patch with its spectral representation before mapping it into the LLM embedding space. Across three language model backbones and six downstream evaluation datasets, Lotus achieves the best average performance with minimal trainable parameters, reaching 59.91% accuracy and outperforming the strongest matched baseline by 3.36%. Our representation analyses further show that Lotus uses the numerical input and preserves temporal structure in its learned patch representations. These results establish forecast grounding as a promising pretraining principle, enabling compact time-series language models to outperform models 25-50 times their size on TSRBench. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/DA2I2-SLM/Lotus

items.title: Rethinking Next-Visit Diagnosis Prediction Beyond Aggregate Metrics: Retrieval--Memory Multi-Agent Adjudication [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Rethinking Next-Visit Diagnosis Prediction Beyond Aggregate Metrics: Retrieval--Memory Multi-Agent Adjudication
items.summary: A new study introduces an evaluation framework for next-visit diagnosis prediction that considers variable diagnosis set sizes, long-tailed labels, and temporal distinctions such as persistent, new, and recurrent diagnoses. The research compares rule-based heuristics, large language model (LLM) prompting, retrieval, memory, and multi-agent methods, finding that simply repeating the last visit's diagnoses often outperforms many LLM approaches. The authors propose LONGINUS, a retrieval-memory multi-agent adjudication framework that combines patient record retrieval with structured memory of patient history. LONGINUS uses cross-view agreement to adjudicate predictions and achieves superior transition-specific performance across multiple datasets and LLM backbones, while maintaining competitive aggregate metrics.

items.title: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Why Pay for Long Reasoning When Rewrite Do Trick? Causal Effects of Reasoning History Compaction on Future Generation and Agent Cost
items.summary: A recent study explores methods to make language model reasoning more efficient by compacting prior reasoning steps into concise summaries, reducing redundancy without retraining the models. This approach was tested on open-weight models and showed that using compacted reasoning histories can shorten future reasoning and decrease repeated verification, particularly in coding tasks. In practical applications involving software agents, this compaction method helped lower operational costs, though its impact on task quality and processing time varied depending on the specific model and compression technique used. The research highlights reasoning history compaction as a promising strategy to enhance reasoning efficiency while maintaining performance.

items.title: Balancing Chain-of-Thought and Answer Supervision for Small Language Models on Medical Question Answering [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Balancing Chain-of-Thought and Answer Supervision for Small Language Models on Medical Question Answering
items.summary: A recent study explores fine-tuning methods for small language models (up to 9 billion parameters) in medical question answering tasks. It compares two chain-of-thought (CoT) supervision techniques: Uniform-across-Sequence (UaS) and Segment-weighted (SwS). Evaluations on multiple-choice and free-text medical QA datasets reveal that SwS generally benefits general-purpose models in multiple-choice tasks, while UaS is more effective for free-text QA across various models. The study also notes that overly long CoT sequences can reduce performance, suggesting that controlling CoT length during training may be advantageous. The findings emphasize tailoring CoT loss weighting strategies to specific task formats and model characteristics rather than applying a uniform approach across all clinical QA tasks.

items.title: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: SLATE: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Long-Horizon API Selection in E-commerce Tool Use
items.summary: Researchers have introduced SLATE, a new large-scale benchmark designed to evaluate the ability of large language models (LLMs) to select and compose appropriate APIs over long sequences in enterprise e-commerce settings. SLATE features a library of around 1,000 tools and uses a deterministic simulator to assess task success based on achieving all reference outcomes, allowing for diverse valid solution paths. Initial experiments with various models, ranging from 3B to 12B parameters, indicate that even the best models complete only 5% of tasks, highlighting the challenge of reliable tool use in complex enterprise environments. The benchmark, simulator, and evaluation tools are publicly available.

items.title: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Whose startup does the AI back? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in LLM-assisted crowdfunding
items.summary: A recent study examined how large language model (LLM) assistants influence backers' decisions in crowdfunding campaigns, focusing on the role of founders' gender and ethnicity. Through an experiment involving seven LLMs evaluating synthetic campaigns with randomized quality and demographic signals, researchers found that by default, founder names had little impact on the models' choices. However, when backers expressed a preference for supporting underrepresented creators, the LLMs showed a consistent tendency to favor founders signaled as Black or female. This behavior suggests that LLM assistants adapt their recommendations based on user preferences rather than inherent biases in their training data.

items.originalTitle: Language Model Augmented Decision Transformer for Multi-Task Offline Reinforcement Learning
items.summary: Researchers have introduced the Language-Model Augmented Decision Transformer (LaMA-DT), a new approach for offline multi-task reinforcement learning. This method leverages a large language model to augment trajectory data and learn policies across multiple tasks using natural language task descriptions. By combining real and augmented data, LaMA-DT improves performance on benchmarks like Meta-World and MuJoCo, especially when data is scarce, enhancing cross-task generalization.

items.title: Swapping the Judge Changes the Ranking: A Preregistered Study of Cross-Provider Replication in LLM-Judged System Comparisons [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Swapping the Judge Changes the Ranking: A Preregistered Study of Cross-Provider Replication in LLM-Judged System Comparisons
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04090v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practitioners who compare systems with an LLM judge and have no human labels often check a conclusion by repeating it with a judge from another provider. We test how far that check can be trusted. In a preregistered study (with a disclosed post-registration reduction of the judge set), five judge models from three providers re-judged 4,000 Chatbot Arena battles (nine systems, 33 system pairs) that carry human votes, each in both response orders. Agreement with the human vote was low at the verdict level (median Cohen's kappa = 0.22), and system rankings did not survive a change of judge: Kendall's tau with the human ranking ranged from 0.17 to 0.89 (median 0.67), so the preregistered hypothesis that rankings remain stable was not supported. Conclusions replicated by two low-cost judges from different providers matched the human conclusion more often than single-judge conclusions (+0.10 precision), but the gain came from filtering out one poorly aligned judge, and replication involving that judge left a conclusion for only 35% of comparisons. Judges that agreed with humans reached a stable conclusion with no more verdicts than human votes required; the others failed to converge on 26-70% of system pairs at the sample sizes tested (up to 100 verdicts per pair). Disagreements with the human vote co-occurred across judges far more often than independence predicts, although a single human vote per battle cannot separate shared judge bias from voter noise.

items.title: Where Do Distilled Students Store Thinking? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Do Distilled Students Store Thinking?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04141v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Small students degrade on large reasoning models' (LRMs') long solutions, so recent work shortens them by interpolating an LRM with a short-answer model at ratio $\lambda$. We ask what student weights retain when this teacher stops thinking, comparing LoRA adapters of three students from three teacher pairs at each $\lambda$. In each pair, the adapters' update subspace shifts most where the teacher stops thinking and solutions shorten most, locating the change without attributing it. We identify a shared adapter subspace tied to thinking-like behavior (reflective markers, monologue format and long solutions). Shared by adapters before that point, it keeps about half (post hoc) while one pair's teacher halves its solutions but keeps its think tag, and largely empties after thinking stops. Removing it largely turns this behavior off for every pair, student and benchmark. Only in that pair and one other student does it leave clearly fewer markers than removing the update's top components; elsewhere, same-energy random directions often nearly match it. Grafted into a short-answer student at twice its weight, it turns early markers (a post hoc count) on, like the whole update, but the student rarely finishes. Our work identifies a weight subspace tied to distilled thinking-like behavior.

items.title: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Length Is Cheap, Competition Is Not: Attention Predicts Context Rot in Retrieval
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04169v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Why do language models fail on long inputs? The common answer is length. We show that, for retrieval, length is cheap and competition is not. On five open models (0.5B to 3B parameters, four families), neutral filler costs nothing: accuracy stays at 0.97 to 1.00, up to 32K tokens on Qwen2.5-1.5B. Statements in the format of the evidence, placed at the same positions, drop it to 0.16 to 0.33. A single statement that gives the queried key a rival value multiplies the loss by 9 to 110, and every additional rival adds to it. Inside the model, one quantity tracks the failure: the attention mass left on the evidence. Across 126,473 trials it explains up to 58% of the variance in loss; log length explains at most 8%. The masked-filler protocol behind the claim that length alone hurts reproduces on MMLU (11 to 18 points lost at 30K tokens), but fails a visible control in retrieval: masking costs 45 accuracy points at 32K tokens, while the same filler left visible costs none. In retrieval, context rot is a competition for attention. We release the probe and all 126K trial-level measurements.

items.title: Tokenizer Myths and Where To Find Them [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Tokenizer Myths and Where To Find Them
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Tokenization is a fundamental component of modern language models: before a model sees data, its tokenizer has already determined how the data appears. We identify and challenge three myths in the tokenization research literature. Myth #1: Bits-Per-Byte (BPB) is agnostic to the tokenizer and/or the vocabulary size: BPB is tokens per byte times bits per token, and the two factors do not cancel; using untrained models, we show that BPB prefers some tokenizers over others: the model has learned nothing, but the tokenizer--model pair has. Myth #2: lower BPB means a better model: On untrained models, BPB strongly prefers some vocabulary sizes, even though accuracy remains at chance, and on real models trained on the same data, BPB correlates weakly with downstream performance. Myth #3: different "tokenizer-agnostic" metrics yield consistent results: The "unigram-normalized loss" is not tokenizer-agnostic; its reported correlation of 0.989 with BPB comes from a confounder and falls to 0.057 once fixed; from the same data the two metrics select different vocabularies at each model size. We present a tokenizer trilemma: no metric can score only the true distribution best, give the same predictions the same score, and tie all untrained models, so choosing a metric is choosing a research question. We conclude with a caution for reading the tokenization literature and a conjecture for future work.

items.title: Constructing a Regional Slang Lexicon for Electricity Demands via Soft-Label Bidirectional Anchoring and Active Learning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Constructing a Regional Slang Lexicon for Electricity Demands via Soft-Label Bidirectional Anchoring and Active Learning
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04231v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Power-grid customer service increasingly relies on community social media, where customers describe outages, billing, and equipment faults in informal regional dialect. Such messages exhibit non-standard morphology, semantic drift, and out-of-vocabulary expressions that make manual lexicon construction costly and degrade conventional NLP tools. We propose a weak-supervision framework constructing a regional slang lexicon from curated dialect anchors and power-domain seed terms. Candidates are generated via Pointwise Mutual Information with soft-label bidirectional anchoring, retaining dialect-anchored terms while recording power-domain relevance as separate metadata, and are scored by combining Sentence-BERT semantic similarity with a jieba-based wordhood measure. Uncertainty-aware active learning with rule-based and retrieval-augmented LLM oracles is applied under three query strategies, and the resulting lexicon is evaluated by a higher-capability LLM calibrated against human expert annotations via Cohen's $\kappa$. On 11,177 real WeChat messages from Yuxi (Yunnan, China), the framework achieves an evaluator-estimated dialect precision of DP~$=$~1.0 with zero false positives. An ablation shows that soft-label layering retains 751\% more candidates than strict power-gating at identical precision, expanding the candidate pool from 41 to 349 terms. Human calibration ($n=46$) yields $\kappa_{\text{dialect}}=1.0$ and $\kappa_{\text{power}}=0.85$. The resulting 25--33-term lexicon, 4--5 of which are power-relevant, provides a preliminary resource for dialect-aware power-grid service NLP.

items.title: Sparse Internal Control of Language Models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sparse Internal Control of Language Models
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04349v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language models are increasingly used in text generation, decision support, and automated interaction, creating a need for localized, reversible, and selective control of their behavior. Activation steering demonstrates that internal interventions can alter the behavior of frozen models, but how to select and evaluate compact, multi-site control interfaces remains an open question. I introduce sparse internal control, a framework for steering target behavior by applying inference-time interventions to a small set of internal model nodes. A local target-controllability formulation characterizes candidate site--direction pairs by their behavioral effects and specifies constraints on target recovery, off-target preservation, and intervention energy. Two complementary selectors instantiate this formulation: Driver-OMP selects nodes for sparse reconstruction of a desired behavioral displacement, while Coverage-Driver favors stable coverage across prompts. I propose a six-axis control-evaluation protocol measuring reachability, signed reversal, dose response, feedback controllability, off-target preservation, and held-out reuse. Exploratory experiments on indirect object identification, MMLU multiple-choice question answering, sentiment steering, and refusal steering provide evidence for the feasibility of steering task-defined behavior through sparse internal interventions. The six-axis evaluation characterizes these interventions beyond target movement, revealing distinct control properties that depend on the task and available direction information. Together, the formulation, reference algorithms, and evaluation protocol provide a foundation for the systematic study and development of internal control methods for language models.

items.title: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Ground Truth Is Not Ground Truth: Automatic Labeling for Hallucination Detection
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04697v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Hallucinations in Large Language Models (LLMs) remain a major challenge, as they can produce misleading, factually incorrect, or unverifiable information, thereby undermining their trustworthiness and reliability. However, reliable ground-truth labels remain a key challenge in evaluating hallucination detectors. Recent studies often construct labels automatically by comparing model generations with reference answers using similarity metrics such as BLEURT. This implicitly treats BLEURT similarity as a proxy for hallucination, despite its English-centric supervision, unbounded score range, and design as a similarity metric rather than a factuality measure, making threshold-based ground-truth construction potentially unreliable. Through comprehensive experiments using 15 automatic supervision judges, seven hallucination detection baselines, two generator models, two QA datasets, and five languages, we demonstrate that detector performance varies substantially with the choice of supervision judge. Human validation reveals substantial differences in labeling reliability, with QGen-9B achieving the lowest overall misclassification rate (12.86%), while BLEURT and BLEURT-n exhibit rates of 47.23% and 47.32%, respectively. Our findings highlight the limitations of automatic similarity-based labeling and the need for more reliable judging methods that better capture semantic and factual correctness.

items.title: ReSI-Math: Exploring Recoverable Capability Frontiers for Efficient Reasoning Improvement [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ReSI-Math: Exploring Recoverable Capability Frontiers for Efficient Reasoning Improvement
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04787v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become an effective approach for improving mathematical reasoning in large language models. However, a fundamental question remains: when a model fails to solve a problem, does it truly lack the underlying capability? In this work, we reveal that direct failure does not necessarily imply inability. Some reasoning failures can be recovered by exploring the model's own trajectories, exposing a recoverable capability frontier: a policy-dependent region where solutions are not reliably generated through direct decoding but can be elicited through trajectory-level search. Based on this observation, we introduce ReSI-Math, a framework that explores recoverable capability frontiers and converts recovered capabilities into data-efficient RLVR supervision. ReSI-Math uses Self-Judge-guided evolutionary search to identify recoverable failures under a fixed policy and adaptively selects frontier problems for sequential RLVR as the policy evolves. On Qwen3-VL-8B, correct-incorrect trajectory crossover produces 272 verifier-confirmed correct offspring from 621 attempts (43.8%). After three sequential one-shot RLVR stages, the MATH500 and WE-MATH average improves from 78.71 to 80.16. Under matched single-problem RLVR, random selection reaches only 53.31 versus 54.16 for frontier-guided Q1.

items.title: One Assistant, Many Memories: Benchmarking Real-World Group Assistance When Recall Is Not Enough [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: One Assistant, Many Memories: Benchmarking Real-World Group Assistance When Recall Is Not Enough
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The value of memory lies not only in recall but in using it to provide appropriate assistance. Recent benchmarks test memory use in personalisation and agentic tasks, but seldom evaluate assistance without fixed answers or integration across multiple participants. Group chats make both challenges more acute: an assistant must integrate information from multiple members, track revisions and conflicts over time, and produce one response for the group. Yet existing group memory benchmarks rely on synthetic conversations and inherit constrained evaluation from general memory benchmarks, focusing on recall against fixed answers or decisions over a closed set. We introduce GroupAssistBench, the first memory benchmark from real-world group conversations with a deployed group assistant, covering 80,299 messages in 50 groups and costing over $53K. Over the same histories, GroupAssistBench evaluates memory recall (L1) with reference answers and memory use (L2) with service requests without fixed answers across single, distributed, and conflicting memories (M1--M3). Requests are verified to require group history, memories are anchored to their sources, and L2 uses tailored rubrics with penalties derived from real user feedback. Across evaluations of frontier models with full context, retrieval methods, and memory systems, the strongest memory system rivals full context on recall but falls far behind on use, especially for distributed and conflicting memories. Together, two additions that relate retrieved memories and bind remembered facts as response constraints bring consistent gains, showing that group memory systems must improve use, not recall alone.

items.title: Shuffled OPSD: When Semantic Consistency Hurts On-Policy Self-Distillation? [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Shuffled OPSD: When Semantic Consistency Hurts On-Policy Self-Distillation?
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04958v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Knowledge distillation improves a student model's reasoning ability through supervision from a teacher. On-policy self-distillation (OPSD) uses the same model as both teacher and student under different contexts: the student generates reasoning trajectories from the question alone, while the teacher additionally receives a complete worked example and provides token-level supervision along those trajectories. Because the problem statement is shared, its content and ordering shape both student generation and teacher feedback. Preserving its semantic structure therefore seems natural, but does it always improve learning? We introduce Shuffled OPSD, which shuffles the words of the shared problem statement while keeping the teacher-only worked example intact. Across three mathematical reasoning benchmarks and three Qwen3 model scales, the method improves mean accuracy over both an intact-target control and Standard OPSD under matched training configurations. The largest gain over Standard OPSD is 3.52 percentage points on Qwen3-1.7B. Further controls show that preserving larger word blocks offers no advantage over word-level shuffling at the evaluated scales, whereas shuffling the teacher-only worked example reduces accuracy at every scale. Cross-problem mixing and target-removal experiments further distinguish the roles of problem content, word order, and teacher context. These results show that disrupting the shared problem statement can improve learning, while disrupting the teacher-only reference hurts performance. They challenge semantic coherence as a universally beneficial principle for OPSD and motivate closer study of how input structure shapes student generation and teacher supervision.

items.title: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they' [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Who is the Pronoun Pro? Comparing LLMs and Humans at Number-Disambiguation of 'they'
items.summary: arXiv:2611.04968v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study evaluates whether large language models (LLMs) can reliably replace or complement human research assistants in linguistically complex annotation. In a controlled annotation task, 73 human annotators (local students and crowdworkers with and without a background in linguistics) and more than 40 LLM configurations number-disambiguated 174 authentic uses of 'they' from Reddit, including innovative and context-sensitive cases. The best LLM, Kimi K3, reached 94.5% accuracy, above the human majority vote (86.2%) and the mean of the top half of human annotators (78.5%); only the single best human annotator scored higher (95.7%). LLMs also offer substantial practical advantages in cost and speed. However, qualitative error analysis reveals a crucial complementarity: human reasoning in low-agreement cases exposes inconsistencies in the annotation typology and thereby improves the methodological framework itself. The study contributes (i) a benchmark-style human-LLM comparison for a semantically demanding task, (ii) transparent cost and time evidence, and (iii) a methodological argument against a purely replacement-oriented view of automation. LLMs are viable for large-scale annotation support in linguistics, but their responsible use requires human critical oversight. The dataset with its gold-standard labels, all human and LLM annotations, and the fully reproducible code are openly available as a Quarto-based, public repository.

items.title: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Right Source Is Not Enough: Understanding History Interference in Speech-LLM Memory
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05124v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Speech large language models retain audio history to support multi-turn conversations. Yet remembering an event does not ensure that its information is used only when relevant. We investigate why irrelevant historical audio changes answers even when the queried event remains represented. Controlled experiments on MOSS-Audio and MiMo-Audio show that historical values direct errors toward specific competing answers, beyond a generic effect of context length. Causal interventions distinguish two paths. In open-ended question answering, most history-value errors disappear when subsequent computation cannot directly access the irrelevant source. In multiple-choice answering, many errors persist: early historical influence is carried by question-candidate states even after direct source access is blocked. Low-dimensional interventions further separate source-role information from answer-value information. Their effects peak at different depths, and changing the source-role signal does not eliminate the causal influence of competing values. On naturally occurring errors, strengthening the queried role and counteracting the historical value each improve answers; their joint intervention gives the greatest recovery. These findings support a failure of downstream evidence use beyond source identification alone: source-role information can influence a decision without exclusively controlling which historical values affect it. Reliable conversational memory therefore requires not only retention and retrieval, but also control over how retained information enters answer computation.

items.title: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Accuracy: What Language-Subspace Interventions Capture, Remove, and Improve
items.summary: arXiv:2611.05278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Language-subspace interventions aim to improve multilingual reasoning by suppressing language-related components in mid-layer activations. Using MATH and MGSM across four open-weight LLMs, we ask three questions: do estimated language subspaces capture translation-associated variation? Does projecting them out remove language information? And do they improve accuracy without compromising response language? For the first question, we build subspaces using the existing Mean-SVD construction and our DiffPCA. Both capture substantial translation-associated variation and show similar patterns across model depth. For the second, we project out each subspace and train linear probes to classify language from the projected activations. The probes still identify language almost perfectly, showing that neither subspace exhaustively captures language information. For the third, we evaluate several intervention configurations on Qwen2.5-7B, by varying subspace creation methods and intervention operators. We find that the intervention that most improves MGSM accuracy sacrifices response-language fidelity, with only one intervention improving joint accuracy--answers that are correct and in the target language--slightly, by 1.60 points. Interestingly, subtle changes in the prompt alone can reproduce the accuracy gains albeit with significant damage to language fidelity. We argue that causal interventions must be judged on more than accuracy, to fully account for language substitution trade-offs.
